schools.summary: Gill makes the shepherd not the Father (as the Targum) but Jehovah the Son, the great, chief, and good Shepherd, omniscient and omnipotent, whom David calls 'my' by the Father's gift; Calvin holds God a shepherd only to those who feel their need, David the king confessing himself a poor sheep.
Augustine has the Church herself speak to Christ, 'the Lord feedeth me, and I shall lack nothing,' the Lord Jesus being the Shepherd under whom she wants for nothing.

Henry recalls David's own shepherd days (Ps. 78:70-71; John 10:11) and his begging to Nabal and Ahimelech, yet 'I shall not want'; Spurgeon dwells on the condescension, on the sweetest word 'my,' and on the present tense, the unconverted being wolves or goats, not sheep.

Ellicott traces the shepherd-image from the individual (Gen. 48:15; 49:24) to the people (Isa. 40:11; Ezek. 34); Keil and Delitzsch admire the arrangement after Ps. 22, hold David the author, and refer it to the rebellion under Absalom.
Clarke reads the psalm as a post-captivity thanksgiving of redeemed captives, and so, against the rest, judges it 'cannot with propriety be attributed to David.'

debates.question: Who wrote the psalm, and on what occasion?

sides.position: David's, composed in the settled prosperity of his kingdom
David's, from the time of the rebellion under Absalom
not David's, but a thanksgiving of the returned captives after the captivity

outliers.note: Reads the psalm allegorically, the Church addressing Christ her Shepherd, rather than as David's own confession.

themes: the occasion and authorship of the psalm

schools.summary: Henry reads the pastures as God's ordinances, never eaten bare, and the still waters as the consolations and joys of the Holy Ghost—not corrupt standing waters nor the troubled sea, but silent purling waters; God makes his saints lie down in contentment.

Gill gives the tender grass a Christward sense—the covenant of grace, Christ's fulness, and the Gospel's doctrines and ordinances (milk for babes, meat for strong men); to lie down denotes satiety, rest, and safety even in the noon of temptation.

Clarke would render 'cottages of turf or sods' (binoth deshe), the safe folds, and reads the still waters as deep waters (Shiloah against Euphrates) figuring captives brought home; Wesley keeps it plain—repose at noon, green for delight and plenty.

Ellicott corrects the tense: the verbs are presents, not futures, describing the poet's customary condition—the freshness of the meadow and coolness of the stream, the completest picture of happiness ever drawn.

debates.question: Is the phrase rightly 'green pastures,' or 'cottages of turf/sods'?

sides.position: 'cottages of turf or sods' (binoth deshe), the sheepfolds

outliers.note: Reads the whole verse through a post-captivity lens—the soft waters of Shiloah against the turbulent Euphrates, captives brought home to their own quiet streams.

themes: the ordinances and consolations of God

schools.summary: Gill offers two senses of 'restoreth'—bringing back the backslider and healing his wanderings, or reviving the fainting soul ready to die with the discoveries of God's love, the promises of his word, and the Spirit's consolations.

Henry leans on the straying sheep (Ps. 119:176)—David's heart smitten, Nathan sent, God restoring his soul, for he will not let his people lie still in sin—yet keeps the healing of the sick and faint too (Exod. 15:26); the paths of righteousness are the truly pleasant way of duty.

Clarke reads the restoring as conversion from sin, and the 'paths' as 'orbits of righteousness' (bemageley tsedek), man a planet round the Sun of righteousness; Wesley glosses 'restoreth' as bringing back from errors, and 'for his name's sake' as for God's glory, not our worth.
Ellicott confirms the verb as refresh, recreate, quicken, and takes 'for his name's sake' to mean God's dealings answer to his own character for great graciousness.

outliers.note: Renders 'paths of righteousness' as 'orbits of righteousness,' making man a secondary planet revolving round the Sun of righteousness, enlightened and warmed only in his proper orbit.

themes: for his name's sake, not our merit

schools.summary: Gill denies the valley means spiritual darkness or God's hidden face (the Lord is with him), taking it of the approach of the grave and the terrors of death—'O death, where is thy sting?'—or, best of all, the severest affliction or dark dispensation of Providence.

Henry hears the courage of a dying saint and finds four mitigations—it is but the shadow, a valley (valleys are fruitful), a walk, and a walk through it to the mountain of spices; death is no terror to Christ's sheep, for 'thou art with me.'

Ellicott presses the reading tsalmuth ('deep gloom, darkness') over tsal-maveth, calling the phrase a forcible synonym for a dark place (the fifteen occurrences) and the valley a deep ravine; Keil and Delitzsch make rod and staff Jahve's own (Mic. 7:14), the one rod doubly named, preserving security and a cheerful spirit.

Clarke holds the shepherd figure to the end—a dark ravine of pitfalls and beasts, safe only because the Shepherd knows every pass—and insists the rod means no correction ('they abuse the text who paraphrase rod correction'); Wesley makes rod and staff one thing, God's pastoral care.
Augustine reads the rod as discipline—'thy discipline, like a rod for a flock and a staff for growing children'—a chastening that has comforted rather than grieved him.

debates.question: Should the word be read tsal-maveth ('shadow of death') or tsalmuth ('deep gloom, darkness')?
Do the shepherd's rod and staff signify correction, or only guidance and defence?

sides.position: guidance and defence, with no idea of correction

themes: the valley of the shadow of death
the rod and staff—defence or discipline
the courage of a dying saint

schools.summary: Ellicott calls the sudden shift from flock to banquet characteristic of Hebrew poetry, glosses 'prepare' as spread or furnish (Prov. 9:2; Isa. 25:6), sets the feast on a secure height before baffled foes, and notes 'my cup runneth over' is literally 'my cup is abundant drink,' the cup a portion (Ps. 16:5).

Clarke declares 'here the second allegory begins'—a host with bounty to feed and power to protect, the oil poured on honoured guests (Luke 7:46), the cup of best wine; Wesley keeps it short—table of plenty, oil the ointment of feasts, the overflowing cup a plentiful portion.

Henry will not let the sheep go—David still a sheep, but the poor man's ewe-lamb fed at its owner's own table (2 Sam. 12:3); the table prepared before him, the cup running over 'enough for myself and my friends too,' the oil for ornament and delight.
Gill spreads the one table over four rooms—providential sufficiency, the fatness of God's house in grace, the table of the Lord under the Gospel, and the feast of heaven foretasted here.

debates.question: Does the imagery leave the shepherd for a host and banquet, or does the sheep remain a sheep?

sides.position: a new, second allegory—the shepherd has become a host, the flock guests at a feast
the sheep is still a sheep, feasted at its owner's own table

themes: in the presence of mine enemies

schools.summary: Henry hears the hope rise—all the streams of mercy following as the rock's water followed Israel, new every morning like the manna (Lam. 3:22-23)—and reads the last clause as David's covenant to dwell and praise, with heaven beyond: 'all this, and heaven too.'

Gill takes goodness and mercy for the free grace of God in Christ and its effects, following even the backslidden; Calvin ends the psalm 'I shall dwell in the house of Jehovah for a length of days,' David's resolve to give himself to God's pure worship.

Keil and Delitzsch make goodness and favour pursue him, driving his pursuers from the field, good spirits sent by Jahve; Ellicott holds the text must read 'I will return and abide,' the house of the Lord hardly anything but the Temple, though some take it figuratively of the divine family.

Clarke reads the verb as veshabti, 'I shall return and abide in the house of the Lord' for length of days—the language of a priest brought home from captivity to serve in the temple and at last dwell in glory.

debates.question: Does the closing verb mean 'I will dwell' or 'I shall return and abide'?

themes: goodness and mercy shall follow me
the house of the LORD for ever
